records.name_note: Sources converge on 'sassafras' as the lead name. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists five entries alphabetically -- Cinnamon Wood, Common Sassafras, Mitten Tree, Sassafras, White Sassafras -- so its first entry reflects alphabetical order rather than a designated primary; NC State's page title repeats the same five names in the same order after the binomial. MoBot's dedicated page for this species displays 'Common Name: sassafras.' RHS's dedicated page is titled 'Sassafras albidum | sassafras' and lists 'ague tree, sassafras tree, white sassafras' separately under 'Other common names.' Because MoBot's and RHS's dedicated pages both lead with 'sassafras,' and NC State's alphabetized list contains 'Sassafras,' that name is used as common_name. 'Cinnamon Wood,' 'Common Sassafras,' and 'Mitten Tree' appear only in NC State's list; 'White Sassafras' appears in NC State's list and, lowercased, in RHS's 'Other common names'; 'ague tree' and 'sassafras tree' appear only in RHS's 'Other common names.'
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poisonous to Humans block rates Poison Severity Low, with Poison Symptoms 'Shown to be a weak carcinogen in experimental animals.', Poison Toxic Principle Safrole, Causes Contact Dermatitis No, and Poison Part: Bark (the only part listed). NC State's Problems field lists Messy and Poisonous to Humans, and its Plant Type field separately carries a 'Poisonous' tag alongside 'Native Plant, Perennial, Shrub, Tree.' NC State's Edibility field reads: 'Teas and drinks are made from the roots. Root beer use to be flavored from the bark of the roots of the sassafras  The leaves are dried and ground to make filé powder, a common thickening ingredient in gumbo.' Missouri Botanical Garden states: 'More recently, sassafras oils have been determined to contain a carcinogenic substance (safrole) and many of the former uses for the oils are now banned by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.' and 'Culinary uses have included: sassafras tea (bark), root beer flavoring (root oil) and a gumbo-thickening agent called filé (stem pith).' The sources disagree on edibility: NC State's Edibility field describes root teas, root-bark root beer flavoring and filé in the present tense, while MoBot frames the same culinary uses in the past and states that many former uses of the oils are now banned by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The severity rating is human-scoped; no admissible source names cats or dogs, and the 'experimental animals' phrase is not scoped to them.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: all admissible toxicity evidence found (NC State's human-scoped Poison block, MoBot's carcinogen note) discusses risk to humans and 'experimental animals' generally; no admissible source names cats or dogs specifically, so per the cat/dog scoping rule this stays null.

UF/IFAS's Light field lists 'full sun, partial sun, or partial shade,' but NC State's and RHS's structured sun fields for this species list only full sun and partial shade (no separate partial-sun tag), so 'part_sun' was excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure per the cross-source rule and is disclosed here instead.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: no source gives species-specific prose stating a sun-hours cap for Sassafras albidum; NC State's '6 or more hours'/'2-6 hours' figures belong to its site-wide light-category legend, which this schema excludes from this field.

chill_damage_f left null: RHS states 'Mature trees are hardy but young trees can suffer frost damage' and rates the species H5 in its Hardiness field, but neither is a stated damage-onset temperature, so no figure was recorded per the no-derivation-from-hardiness-ratings rule.

records.name_note: NC State lists seven common names alphabetically (American Hornbeam, Blue Beech, Hornbeam, Ironwood, Musclewood, Muscle Wood, Water Beech); the first, American Hornbeam, is also the first name in the page title and the name its description prose uses. MoBot displays a single field, 'Common Name: American hornbeam' (a longer list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's markup and is not quoted). RHS gives American hornbeam as its plant-profile subtitle and page-title common name, with blue beech, ironwood and water beech only under Other common names. UF/IFAS titles its fact sheet 'Carpinus caroliniana: American Hornbeam' and calls the species Ironwood throughout its prose. NC State's prose explains musclewood: 'The common name musclewood comes from the appearance of the smooth bark over branches with sinewy fluting that resembles muscles.' Ironwood is shared with Ostrya virginiana, whose own NC State page lists Ironwood among its common names (and which NC State's 'is often confused with' module names), so this catalog treats Ironwood as a collision name rather than a lead. common_name is American Hornbeam.
unknowns: No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs for this species; NC State's page carries no Poison block (its Plant Type/Problems tags list only disease issues, no 'Poisonous' tag), so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than guessed.

No admissible source states a specific chill-damage onset temperature, day/night temperature ranges, humidity percentage range, or light footcandle values for this species (it is an outdoor landscape/native tree, not treated as a houseplant by any source), so chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max are all left null.

NC State's Soil pH field lists an open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band and a closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band. Per the rule requiring the closed band's floor/ceiling to be checked against RHS in both directions, RHS's Soil pH field lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral as all acceptable, so both soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null.

MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium,' a mid-scale value that per the rules cannot support water_regime=keep_moist; no admissible source frames watering for this in-ground tree with an explicit directive beyond that mid-scale tag, so water_regime is left null (MoBot's Culture prose 'Easily grown in average, medium moisture soil... Prefers moist, organically rich soils' likewise stops short of a clear watering directive). water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are also left null, consistent with the rule that day-interval/dry-down fields stay null for an in-ground tree unless a source frames watering that way.
No admissible source gives a fertilizing interval, active months, or dilution strength for this species, so all three fertilize_* fields are left null.

is_houseplant is set to false based on NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone listing (3a-9b) and this species' identity throughout all admissible sources as a cold-hardy native understory tree grown in the landscape, not marketed or described as an indoor houseplant by any admissible source.

outdoor_sun_exposure carries part_shade and full_shade: part_shade is the one value all four sources carry; full_shade rests on both North American structured fields (NC State's Light field lists only Deep shade and Partial Shade; MoBot's Sun field reads Part shade to full shade) plus NC State's 'does well in heavy shade' and UF/IFAS's 'total shade' prose, with RHS's Position and UF/IFAS's Light requirement field stopping at partial shade; full_sun is disclosed, not carried -- it appears in RHS's Position and UF/IFAS's Light requirement field but is excluded by both North American structured fields for a shade-tolerant understory tree.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's browser-title parenthetical and its Common Name(s) field carry the same eight entries in the same alphabetized order (American Fringetree, American Fringe Tree, Fringetree, Fringe Tree, Grancy Greybeard, Old Man's Beard, Sweetheart Tree, White Fringetree); NC State's body prose opens 'Fringetree is a small, deciduous tree in the olive family (Oleaceae).' and uses the one-word 'Fringetree' throughout. MoBot's rendered 'Common Name:' field carries a single value, 'fringe tree'; a longer list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's attribute markup, so it is not quoted here, and MoBot's own prose says 'commonly called fringetree'. RHS's plant-profile subtitle gives 'fringe tree' (its H1 is the botanical name alone; its browser title reads 'Chionanthus virginicus | fringe tree'), with 'North American fringe tree, old man's beard, poison ash, Virginian snow flower' listed separately under 'Other common names.' UF/IFAS ST161 reads 'Common name(s): Fringetree, Old-Mans-Beard.' Four dedicated single-species sources carry an affirmative common-name value and they split two-two: MoBot and RHS lead with 'fringe tree,' NC State's prose and UF/IFAS with the one-word 'Fringetree.' common_name is set to 'Fringe Tree' on the strength of the two structured common-name fields that name a single lead value; 'Fringetree,' 'White Fringetree,' and 'Old Man's Beard' are also in active use across these sources and are not discarded, just not primary.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's Plant Type field does not include 'Poisonous' and the page has no Poison block; Clemson's fringetree factsheet, UF/IFAS's ST161 publication, and RHS's plant profile were all checked and none of them state a toxicity or pet-safety claim for this species. RHS does list 'poison ash' as one of its Other common names, which hints at a folk toxicity association, but that is a name only, not a toxicity statement, so it cannot support toxic_to_pets.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering statement or structured moisture field for this species that maps to one of the four enum values. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium,' which per the schema rules is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist; it is noted here only as a disclosed counterpoint. Clemson and UF/IFAS describe soil moisture preference ('prefers moist... soils'; 'occasionally wet') but not a watering regime.

soil_ph_min left null though NC State's Soil pH field reads 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)': RHS's Soil pH field for this species reads 'Acid' (acid soils listed as acceptable), so per the schema rule the floor read off NC State's closed band is not used and soil_ph_min is left null instead. soil_ph_max is retained at 8.0 because RHS does not list alkaline soils as acceptable for this species.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and all fertilize_* fields left null: this is an in-ground landscape tree and no source frames its care in dry-down, day-interval, or fertilizer-schedule terms.

direct_sun_hours_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, day_f/night_f fields, chill_damage_f, and cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source gives species-specific numeric values for these; NC State's Light field only carries its generic site-wide hour legend, which the schema rules exclude as a source for direct_sun_hours_max.

Not a schema field, but decision-relevant: NC State's body prose states the species is functionally unisexual/dioecious ('The flowers have both male and female parts but are functionally unisexual...'), and Clemson notes 'Female fringetrees bear attractive fruit if male plants are nearby' -- fruit set requires a male plant nearby.

Clemson's page (hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/fringetree/) is a genus factsheet covering both native Chionanthus virginicus and Chinese fringetree (Chionanthus retusus) side by side, not a dedicated single-species page; only the C. virginicus-specific passages were used here.

MoBot's Common Names tooltip was located in the page's onmouseover/onclick attribute markup but was not opened/rendered as a live popup by this research pass, so per instructions its content is not quoted; the single rendered 'Common Name: fringe tree' field was cited instead.

2026-09-03 landing: name_note replaced with the auditor's corrected wording -- the invented 'three or more entries' rule is gone, the count of affirmative common-name sources is four (a two-two split), and UF/IFAS's field, MoBot's one-word prose and NC State's browser title are now cited.

records.name_note: Sources agree on the working name but split on the structured lead. NC State's Common Name(s) list orders 'Common Pawpaw' before 'Pawpaw', matching the page title's parenthetical 'Asimina triloba (Common Pawpaw, Pawpaw)', while NC State's own body prose calls the species 'Pawpaw' and never 'Common Pawpaw' in running text. Clemson's dedicated factsheet leads with 'Pawpaw' in its title and H1; MoBot's Common Name field reads 'pawpaw'; RHS's plant-profile subtitle reads 'pawpaw'. Given that three of the four admissible sources -- Clemson, MoBot and RHS -- lead with 'Pawpaw'/'pawpaw', that name is used here as common_name; NC State, which also has a dedicated page for this species, is the one source that lists 'Common Pawpaw' first, in a two-item list matching its page-title parenthetical, while its own body prose uses only 'Pawpaw'.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's structured Poison block for Asimina triloba sits under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading; the page's Problems list carries two tags -- 'Contact Dermatitis' and 'Poisonous to Humans' -- and its Plant Type field lists both 'Edible' and 'Poisonous'. The block rates Poison Severity as Low, gives Poison Toxic Principle as acetogenins, lists Causes Contact Dermatitis as Yes, and gives the full Poison Part list as Fruits, Leaves, Seeds, Stems, with Poison Symptoms reading: 'Stomach and intestinal pain from eating the fruit skin or seeds. Skin irritation from handling fruit. Do not consume leaves or stems.' NC State's Edibility field adds a quantity limit: 'Mature fruits have a banana custard flavor. Raw fruits can be eaten in small quantities but can cause stomach/skin irritation in some people.' Its description carries a handling warning: 'It is recommended to wear gloves when harvesting as contact dermatitis has been known to occur.' Clemson's factsheet scopes its caution to the seeds and green peel: 'Seeds and the green peel (skin) contain alkaloids that are emetic (which causes vomiting); therefore, the seeds and peel should not be consumed.' Missouri Botanical Garden notes the fruit is 'frequently eaten raw or used in ice creams or pies, although they can produce nausea in some people.' Sources differ on scope: Clemson names only seeds and peel, while NC State's Poison Part list includes Fruits as a whole and its Edibility field limits even ripe raw fruit to small quantities. No admissible source scopes any of this toxicity information to cats or dogs.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets is left null: NC State's Poison block for pawpaw is filed under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' problem tag with no accompanying 'Problem for Cats' or 'Problem for Dogs' tag, and no other admissible source (Clemson, MoBot, RHS) scopes toxicity to cats or dogs specifically, so cat/dog-scoped evidence was not found.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_shade: NC State's structured Light field lists 'Deep shade' in addition to Full sun and Partial Shade, but neither RHS (Position: Full sun only) nor MoBot (Sun: Full sun to part shade) supports a full-shade tolerance, so it was left out per the cross-source rule and is disclosed here.

humidity_need/humidity_pct are left null: no admissible source states a humidity requirement for pawpaw. NC State lists 'Humidity' only as a 'Resistance To Challenges' tolerance tag, not a stated need.

direct_sun_hours_max and light_fc fields are left null: no admissible source gives species-specific direct-sun-hour or footcandle prose; NC State's Light field only carries its site-wide legend hour ranges (6+ hours for Full sun, 2-6 for Partial Shade, <2 for Deep shade), which per instructions may not be used as species-specific direct_sun_hours_max.

chill_damage_f is left null: Clemson notes South Carolina growers should avoid coastal climates because pawpaw needs 'winter chilling,' and that some southern-range selections 'likely only require 400-600 chill hours,' but this is a chill-hour dormancy/fruiting requirement, not a damage-onset temperature in °F, so it does not populate chill_damage_f.
day_f/night_f temperature range fields are left null: no admissible source gives daytime or nighttime temperature guidance for pawpaw.

water_regime is left null: MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium to wet' (mid-to-wet, not a clean match to any of the four enum values), and Clemson only frames watering around the establishment period ('providing water when needed will be sufficient until trees begin to grow'), so no source frames pawpaw's ongoing watering the way the enum requires.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: Clemson recommends 'an annual spring broadcast of a balanced granular fertilizer, such as 10-10-10,' but gives no literal day-interval number or specific month(s), and 10-10-10 is an NPK formulation rather than a dilution/strength fraction, so none of the three fields could be populated.
